newsitem.title: HUNGARY: VW WIDENS AUTO SALES LEAD IN CEN. EUROPE.
newsitem.headline: VW WIDENS AUTO SALES LEAD IN CEN. EUROPE.

text.p: Volkswagen AG continued to widen its lead in central Europe's booming market for new autos in May, while Daewoo Group overtook Fiat SPA for second place, according to a monthly Reuters survey.
"Volkswagen is a step ahead of Daewoo and Fiat -- its products are technically superior," auto analyst Vic Heylen told Reuters from his office in Antwerp, Belgium.
"Fiat also might have over-concentrated on one market -- Poland. They will have to expand their presence beyond there."
Volkswagen (VW) upped its lead nine percent from April in countries in the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) -- the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
VW, which already increased its lead 122 percent in April from March, outsold its closest rival, Daewoo, 23,120 units to 17,638 units.
Daewoo, which has become a major CEFTA power by buying several state-owned automakers in the region, had held the third position throughout the year.

The Korean conglomerate, which also builds TVs and operates banks in central Europe, overtook a weakening Fiat, whose sales fell 11.1 percent to 15,610 units in May 1997 from 17,556 units in May 1996.

Analysts said Daewoo's position will continue to improve. In July, CEFTA admitted Romania, where Daewoo sold nearly 2,000 units a month in 1996 on the strength of its large factory there. In contrast, Fiat and VW each sold under 250 units in Romania all last year.
No other automaker sold over 7,000 units in CEFTA in May.
Trailing the Big Three of central Europe were General Motors Corp selling 6,654 units, Renault SA selling 4,650 units, Ford Motor Co selling 4,437 units and PSA Peugeot Citroen selling 4,158 units.

VW -- including the Audi, SEAT, Skoda and VW brands -- raced ahead of Fiat at the end of 1996. The German automotive group has kept the lead except in February, when it slipped behind the Italian automaker.
Fiat -- including Alfa Romeo, Fiat, Iveco, Lancia and several specialty brands -- had been the annual leader in CEFTA sales from the time the trade pact formed in 1993 through 1995.
The data, based on information that Reuters obtained from a variety of sources, include cars, minibuses, pickups, vans and other four-wheeled motor vehicles not over five tonnes in gross weight.
Overall, CEFTA sales growth remained below its all-time peak in 1996, when sales rose 39.5 percent to 842,577 units.
But the market remained buoyant, expanding 16.0 percent to 86,231 units in May 1997 from 74,362 units in May 1996.

And CEFTA continued to look dynamic compared to western Europe, where year-on-year sales fell 1.9 percent in May 1997, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers Association, known by its French acronym ACEA.

VW has built its lead on a broad presence in the region. The German automotive group still centers its CEFTA strategy upon Czech brand Skoda, but it also plans to assemble models from each of its brands throughout central Europe.
VW assembles SEATs and Skodas in Poland as well as VWs in Poland and Slovakia. By mid-1998, it plans to start assembling Audis in Hungary.
Fiat has focused more narrowly on CEFTA. It owns the region's biggest car factory in Poland, but it builds no vehicles elsewhere in central Europe.

The Italian conglomerate sells twice as many brands as VW in CEFTA. But many of these brands, such as Ferrari and Maserati, feature high-priced specialty cars that attract only a small number of customers.
As a result, the Fiat brand provided 97.9 percent of the Italian group's CEFTA sales in May, while Skodas accounted for only 70.9 percent of VW's sales.
Daewoo, which plans to build over 500,000 vehicles a year in central Europe by 2000, has led a Korean blitz on the region in the mid-1990s that has produced stunning results, analysts said.
In May, Korean automakers sold 19,003 units in five countries in central Europe, not far behind the 24,090 units they sold in 18 countries in western Europe, ACEA reported.
